newsitem.title: KUWAIT: U.S. tells Kuwait compatibility key to defence.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tells Kuwait compatibility key to defence.

text.p: The United States told Kuwait on Monday it should give great importance to compatibility when buying arms.

"We discussed the need for interoperability and place a key premium on the interoperability of our systems," U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen told a joint news conference with his Kuwaiti counterpart Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah.

Sheikh Salem stressed that Kuwait had not concluded any deal for a requirement for up to three battalions of tracked self-propelled 155mm guns which experts said could be worth $600 million depending on specification and training.
"We agreed that if we purchase anything from the United States it has to be within our capability and readiness in order to use the equipment," he added.
The minister said his tiny state was eager to buy top-of-the-line arms "but you do not have the mankind (manpower) to use it. So in this respect your decision is not the proper one."
Diplomatic and industry sources earlier told Reuters that Kuwait's key Western allies were expected to press the Gulf Arab state to reverse a decision to buy the guns from China.

There has been no official announcement on the deal but the sources said a Kuwaiti military committee had recently picked the Chinese to equip a Kuwait Land Forces battalion with 18 howitzers with an option for a second battalion.

But the state has apparently sent the recommendation back to the committee in recent days with some technical questions. Diplomatic sources expect British Foreign Office Minister Derek Fatchett, due to arrive on June 23, to raise the issue of the guns.

In competition with China, Washington, which led the 1991 Gulf War alliance, hopes to sell Kuwait its M109 A6 Paladin. The British are pushing hard to sell the Desert AS90. South Africa has offered its wheeled LIW 155mm G6.
The Paladin is deployed in Kuwait with U.S. forces which often fire the gun in joint exercises.
Since it was freed from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, Kuwait has had a policy of awarding key weapons contracts to the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.

Kuwait has defence and cooperation pacts with China, Russia, France, Britain and the United States. All but China have won arms contracts since the Gulf War but Beijing has secured other lucrative state deals.
